4. Quit your browser, relaunch it, and go back to the FDF. Is your red or blue theme (wherever you last left it) still selected?

Yes, it is\!

5. How is the current theme transmitted between the browser and the FDF server?

When the browser first visits the site and the theme is set. The FDF server sends a Set-Cookie header allowing the browser to save the current theme. As you navigate through the website, the browser sends a Cookie header containing the value theme=\[current theme\]. This lets the FDF server maintain the current theme across different pages on the website.  
Similarly, if you visit the site again at a later time and the cookie hasn’t expired yet. The browser sends a Cookie header with the last theme that it set.

6. When you change the theme, how is the change transmitted between the browser and the FDF server?

The browser first sends a GET request with the desired theme set as a parameter in the URL. The FDF server then sets the new theme and sends a Set-Cookie header to the browser with the value of the new theme. The browser then stores that cookie.

7. How could you use your browser's Inspector to change the FDF theme without using the FDF's Theme menu?

By changing the value in the stored cookie in the Inspector tab. Then refreshing the page.

8. How could you use Burpsuite's Proxy tool to change the FDF theme without using the FDF's Theme menu?

Refresh the page and then change the value in the Cookie header and forward that instead.

## Part 2: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

### Steps to take:

- Login to the FDF as Alice (alice@example.com, password: alice) or Bob (bob@example.com, password: bob) or Eve (go ahead, guess her email and password\!).

- Make a post and view your post by clicking on its title in the list of posts at the bottom of the page. Please include your initials in the title of your post like I did with my "\[JO\]" titles.

- Go back to the FDF home page.

- Click on each of Moriarty's posts and pay attention. What happens?

- Study the source code of each of Moriarty's posts. It's shown on the post details page itself, but you should also right-click on the background and select View Page Source to take a look at the raw HTML. Or, alternatively, you can select the Elements tab in the browser Inspector and take a look at the source. Regardless, your goal is to figure out how Moriarty made the FDF behave surprisingly.

- Experiment making your own posts as Alice, Bob, or Eve. Make the title descriptive of what you're trying to do, but fool around in the post body however you want to. (If you're unfamiliar with HTML, CSS, and Javascript, you may want to grab a classmate who knows about those things to help you implement your nefarious plans.)

### Questions:

1. Provide a diagram and/or a step-by-step description of the nature and timing of Moriarty's attack on users of the FDF. Note that some of the relevant actions may happen long before other actions.

- Moriarty creates a post that includes some javascript on his machine
- The post is submitted and added to the server
- The post appears on the list of posts on the homepage of the forum
- Some time passes (years, weeks, months, days, minutes) and a different user clicks on Moriarty's post and the javascript that was in the post gets run in the browser on that user's machine.
- Thus, Moriarty is able to execute code on another user's machine without ever needing to have access to their machine.

2. Describe an XSS attack that is more virulent than Moriarty's "turn something red" and "pop up a message" attacks. Think about what kinds of things the Javascript might have access to via Alice's browser when Alice views the attacker's post.

- User creates a post that contains javascript to redirect the user to another page using a harmless title
- The post gets added to the forum
- A different user clicks on the post and is redirected to their malicious site (or in my case back to the homepage)

3. Do it again: describe a second attack that is more virulent than Moriarty's, but that's substantially different from your first idea.

- The attacker could also log the user out of their account by resetting the session cookie. (I wasn’t able to figure it out, but I figure if you can reset the theme cookie it would also be possible to reset the session cookie”)
- This would be a big nuisance and could act as a denial of service attack especially if they populate the forum with tons of fake posts that log you out.

4. What techniques can the server or the browser use to prevent what Moriarty is doing?

- The server could sanitize the input by forcing the post to be text rather than immediately placing it in the document.
- They could also go through and look for special characters and replace them accordingly.
